title: Andenes Y Cierres
label: ch:es-via
canDo: I can read the signs that decide where I may walk: a platform number, a shop shut for now, a street severed, and an office that has moved.

payoff.summary: Read the notice or message this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
payoff.note: Wordlist derived from the A2 mock audit, as in 431-438. THE CHAPTER SEPARATES THREE SIGNS ENGLISH COLLAPSES INTO 'CLOSED': cerrado is shut for now and will reopen; cortada means the route is severed, so go round; trasladado means it is open somewhere else and there is an address underneath. Picking the wrong one costs a learner an afternoon on a pavement. cerrado also pairs the REGULAR participle against abrir's irregular abierto (ES-GRAMMAR-ABIERTO-03), which sits on the other side of the same shop door. IT ALSO TEACHES THE LIMIT OF ETYMOLOGY: anden and tirar both carry roots: [] because their origin is genuinely unsettled, and the lessons say so rather than inventing a derivation. Every other word in 431-439 comes apart; these two do not, and a course that produced an etymology for every word would be making some of them up. tirar also carries the door-sign reversal -- TIRAR means PULL, not throw -- which catches every English speaker once.
